item.title: NFL is reviewing the Jordan Elliott situation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Titans promptly notified the league office regarding gun incident at facility.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL has essentially confirmed that former Titans defensive tackle Jordan Elliott went to his car to get a gun last week, after an altercation at practice. Beyond prompting the Titans to cut Elliott, the league is investigating the situation.

In response to this question posed to an NFL spokesperson via email on Wednesday morning — "Is he facing league scrutiny given the report that he went to retrieve a gun from car?" — the league said, "Yes. The club promptly notified the league of the matter which is under review."

A source with a team other than the Titans called the incident an "egregious conduct violation to have a gun at an NFL facility," and that the rule is (or at least is required to be) posted in every team facility, in multiple locations.

"You aren’t allowed to have one in your car if your car is parked inside an NFL facility," the source said. "So I think it’s fairly certain that Ellliott will be suspended if and when he signs with a team."

Fortunately, an inherently dangerous situation did not result in a tragedy. The message to all other players is clear. If you have a gun, always leave it at home before you drive to work.

item.title: Giants will release Najee Harris
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: On Sunday, Giants running back Najee Harris expressed concern about the distribution of touches in the team's ground game.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, Giants running back Najee Harris expressed concern about the distribution of touches in the team's ground game. He'll now get none at all.

Via Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, the Giants are releasing Harris.

In five games with one start in New York, Harris had 31 attempts for 99 yards. In Sunday's loss to the Saints, Harris had four carries for two yards on 11 snaps.

Before the game, it was reported that Harris was expected to take on a larger role.

The framing of the report — that the Giants "are releasing" Harris — could be an effort to get someone to try to trade for his one-year, $1.215 million contract.

Either way, he's out with the Giants. And it's hard not to think it was a reaction to his candid criticism of the running game.

“It’s hard to get in a rhythm with one or two plays," Harris said. "The first couple runs will be like, ‘OK, how are they playing it?’ And then the next ones will be, ‘OK, this is how you attack it.’ But if you’re getting a play here and then get taken out for a series, there’s nothing you could do. That’s why I’m saying, ‘I don’t know.’ I’ve never been through none of this before.”

A first-round pick in 2021, Harris had four straight 1,000-yard seasons in Pittsburgh. He tore an Achilles tendon after only three games with the Chargers in 2025, after an offseason fireworks mishap.

item.title: NFL will have heightened security for game in Paris after recent civil unrest
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The game in Paris between the Steelers and Saints will go on as scheduled Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The game in Paris between the Steelers and Saints will go on as scheduled Sunday. The NFL, though, said it will heighten security in light of the civil unrest in the French capital.

NFL executive Peter O'Reilly said Tuesday the league is coordinating with the U.S. State Department and Parisian and national authorities overseas.

“There’s nothing more important from our standpoint than the teams’ security, the fans’ security — everybody involved with this game,” O’Reilly said at the fall league meetings, via the Associated Press. “Obviously being very vigilant in everything we do, in all of our planning on an hour-by-hour basis, working closely with the two teams.”

Rioting erupted across France on Saturday as demonstrators protested rising living costs and declining public services. It was the country's worst civil unrest in years, with violence and looting in major cities as rioters clashed with police.

The NFL did not consider moving the game, which is being played at Stade de France outside of Paris in Saint-Denis. It marks the NFL's first game in France.

"We feel confident that we would not have any impact on the broader resources needed," O'Reilly said. “That’s always top of mind for us, and we feel confident that we wouldn’t be depleting resources in a negative way around this game.”

The Saints flew to Paris after their victory over the Giants on Sunday. The Steelers will travel later this week.

item.title: Todd Monken: We're better with Jerry Jeudy than we are without him
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Jerry Jeudy has ostensibly been passed on Cleveland's depth chart by the team's rookie receivers, KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston.
item.content:encoded:
Jerry Jeudy has ostensibly been passed on Cleveland's depth chart by the team's rookie receivers, KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston.

But in the Browns' last two wins, Jeudy has been the one to come up with significant late-game receptions to put the club in a position to win.

On Sunday, it was a 33-yard catch-and-run on third-and-5 to set up Andre Szmyt for a game-winning field goal.

Jeudy finished the game with a team-leading 69 yards on four catches.

“I mean, we’re better with Jerry than we are without Jerry,” head coach Todd Monken said in his Monday news conference, via transcript from the team. “And I think we’re doing a better job of getting him involved and trying to find the places where we can use Jerry. And it hasn’t been easy, as I said before.

“But he’s handled it well the last few weeks, and you can see it with the confidence playing, the juice he has. And that’s the biggest thing, from practice to the games, carrying that over.”

Jeudy did not have a reception in Cleveland’s Week 2 and Week 3 victories, getting just one target over that span. But over the last three games, he’s caught 10 passes for 124 yards.

He’s now No. 4 on the club with a total of 150 receiving yards this season, behind Boston, Concepcion, and tight end Harold Fannin.

item.title: What's next for Dan Quinn?
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: At the end of the first half of Monday night's game, with the Commanders down 20-3 and coach Dan Quinn going viral based on a lip-reading clip that was being widely interpreted as him not realizing it was fourth down (after a failed fourth-down play), it looked like Quinn was on track to get fired after the game.
item.content:encoded:
At the end of the first half of Monday night's game, with the Commanders down 20-3 and coach Dan Quinn going viral based on a lip-reading clip that was being widely interpreted as him not realizing it was fourth down (after a failed fourth-down play), it looked like Quinn was on track to get fired after the game.

Then came the second half, and an effort by the Commanders that made the final score (23-17) far more respectable.

So now owner Josh Harris has a decision to make. One week removed from the humiliating clock debacle and entering the bye week, will Harris make a change?

Even with the six-point margin, the Commanders remain 1-4-1. Working in Quinn's favor is the fact that the division is still there to be had, if they can turn it around.

The other consideration is that the bump from making an interim hire could also give the team the kind of wakeup call that could carry them to an NFC East title. (At that point, however, it would be difficult to not reward the interim coach by giving him the permanent job.)

There's a mini-bye looming, between the Week 10 Thursday night game against the Giants and the Week 11 Monday night game against the Bengals. Maybe Harris will decide to kick the can, giving the Commanders three more games (Eagles, Rams, at Giants) before making a final decision.

item.title: PFT's Week 7 2026 NFL power rankings
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Niners stay on top.
item.content:encoded:
1. 49ers (last week No. 1; 6-0): Kyle Shanahan is having his best year yet.

2. Chiefs (No. 2; 5-0): Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III is the NFL MVP so far.

3. Bills (No. 4; 5-1): The defense still needs plenty of work.

4. Jaguars (No. 3; 4-2): They're finally getting a return on the Travis Hunter investment.

5. Vikings (No. 6; 5-0): Some tough games are coming.

6. Broncos (No. 7; 4-2): They'll go as far as the offense can take them.

7. Seahawks (No. 5; 3-3): They should've kept Kenneth Walker III.

8. Patriots (No. 9; 4-2): The injuries are piling up before a short-week trip to Chicago.

9. Packers (No. 11; 4-2): They're getting Josh Jacobs back at a perfect time.

10. Bears (No. 15; 4-2): A franchise quarterback makes all the difference.

11. Browns (No. 12 (tie); 4-2): Szmyt happens, in the bad way before the good way.

12. Ravens (No. 8; 4-2): They need Lamar Jackson back in the lineup.

13. Steelers (No. 12 (tie); 4-2): Time to get Le Torchon Terrible ready.

14. Bengals (No. 12 (tie); 3-2): They need to start stacking some wins.

15. Panthers (No. 18; 3-2): Two years after being benched, Bryce Young is earning a big contract.

16. Raiders (No. 16; 3-3): Can the most popular team in L.A. send the Rams into a deeper hole?

17. Rams (No. 10; 2-4): The 13th overall pick should've been used on a receiver.

18. Lions (No. 21; 3-2): The next two games (Packers, Vikings) could shape the season.

19. Texans (No. 24; 2-4): They're in the same position they were in a year ago, but with a better record in the division.

20. Saints (No. 25; 2-4): The Gayle Benson bounce is real.

21. Giants (No. 17; 3-2-1): J.J. McCarthy time is coming.

22. Cardinals (No. 29; 2-4): Maybe they should move to L.A.

23. Cowboys (No. 20; 2-4): Cheap does as cheap is.

24. Falcons (No. 22; 2-4): They should change their name to the Vampires.

25. Eagles (No. 19; 2-4): The questions about the handling of Jalen Hurts won't be going away, no matter how badly they want them to.

26. Titans (No. 31; 1-5): Can they build on their unlikely win in Indy?

27. Colts (No. 23; 2-4): Is a fire sale coming?

28. Jets (No. 26; 2-4): With the Dolphins coming to town, Sunday becomes a must-win game.

29. Buccaneers (No. 27; 1-5): If they'd known what Jalon Daniels can do, would they have extended Baker Mayfield?

30. Commanders (No. 28; 1-4-1): Dan Quinn's time is up. And the end result likely won't be a tie.

31. Dolphins (No. 32; 0-5): "Thank you, Mike McDaniel."

32. Chargers (No. 30; 0-6): Has any team ever failed so badly to live up to their preseason expectations?

item.title: Ben Johnson: Drake Maye is an elite deep ball thrower, can crush you with his legs
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: When the Bears play the Patriots on Thursday night, it will be the first time Ben Johnson coaches against quarterback Drake Maye.
item.content:encoded:
When the Bears play the Patriots on Thursday night, it will be the first time Ben Johnson coaches against quarterback Drake Maye.

Asked about Maye in his Tuesday press conference, Johnson was highly complimentary of the quarterback’s multi-faceted skill set.

“Well, it's a dangerous combination of a guy that's an elite deep ball thrower along with, he can crush you with his legs. I think that combination is deadly,” Johnson said, via transcript from the team. “It's really picked up steam over these last three games. You can see that their offense is putting up points in bunches right now — three-game winning streak and a ton of explosive plays throughout. When you look at it that way, he's a big challenge.

“[Patriots OC] Josh McDaniels does a great job just making sure he puts those guys in the right spots. Even if they're down some O-linemen, he'll do a great job making sure he has that in mind and, showcases what the rest of their guys can do.”

While Maye had a rough start to the season, he’s performed better over the last three game, particularly the last two. After throwing for 374 yards with four touchdowns against Las Vegas in Week 5, he threw for 235 with three TDs in Sunday’s victory over the Jets.

Overall, Maye has completed 63.9 percent of his passes this season for 1,463 yards with 11 touchdowns and seven interceptions. He’s also rushed for 185 yards with a TD.

item.title: Diego Pavia expresses intention to play in the UFL
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Former Vanderbilt quarterback Diego Pavia, who finished second in the Heisman Trophy voting last year, currently is a man without a team.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vanderbilt quarterback Diego Pavia, who finished second in the Heisman Trophy voting last year, currently is a man without a team. That will apparently be changing in 2027.

Pavia said on Tuesday night that he plans to join the UFL.

"[M]y agent . . . and the UFL are currently in negotiations to make this happen!" Pavia tweeted. "[W]hatever team I end up at, I can promise you one thing- You will get everything I got."

Pavia signed with the Ravens after going undrafted in April. He was cut just before the opening of training camp.

The UFL draft is set for November 18. The Columbus Aviators hold the first pick, followed by the new, to-be-named team in Colorado. Which was relocated from Dallas, after the Dallas franchise was swapped with Houston.

Pavia's presence could give the UFL the boost it needs, from a ratings and P.R. perspective. Still, the UFL needs to do plenty more work to get to where it wants to be. It needs to work harder, and it needs to work smarter. On Sunday, for example, the spring league announced — during NFL games — that the team relocated from Birmingham to Rhode Island will be named the Breakers.

Regardless of the existing depth chart at the position, every team should want Pavia. He'll sell tickets. He'll create buzz. He'll help the UFL be something more than a collection of unknowns and marginally recognizable names.

Along the way, Pavia will get the kind of opportunities that could, if maximized, secure an opportunity in the NFL. Like plenty of other UFL players have done.

item.title: Dan Quinn tells Jayden Daniels to "take your shot" even when there's a penalty flag on the field
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: One of the lingering questions from this week's Monday Night Football relates to the perception that Commanders coach Dan Quinn didn't know his team was facing a fourth-and-two play from the San Francisco 13 when it was, you know, facing a fourth-and-two play from the San Francisco 13.
item.content:encoded:
One of the lingering questions from this week's Monday Night Football relates to the perception that Commanders coach Dan Quinn didn't know his team was facing a fourth-and-two play from the San Francisco 13 when it was, you know, facing a fourth-and-two play from the San Francisco 13.

After the game ended, Quinn (who was ready to address the viral lip-reading moment) said he "definitely" knew it was fourth down, before essentially acknowledging that he didn't instantly realize a post-snap foul on the offense could be declined.

At his day-after press conference (which, by virtue of the fact that it happened means he hasn't been fired, yet), Quinn addressed the decision of Jayden Daniels to throw the ball to a wide open Sourdough Sam, who was standing in his 49ers mascot costume well beyond the back of the end zone.

"Even when you know there's a penalty, like, you still take your shot, man, to go throw it, complete it, you don't know if it's gonna get picked up," Quinn said regarding his message to Daniels.

It's more than the flag getting picked up. A penalty on the offense, coupled with the decision of the officials to not stop the play, didn't alleviate the obligation to get a first down. It remained a "gotta have it" play. It didn't become an occasion to throw the ball away.

Daniels addressed the situation in his post-game press conference.

"I've just got to execute better in that situation regardless of a flag or not," Daniels said. "You know, fourth down . . . I have to be better, you know, in that spot."

But it wasn't a matter of better execution. It was a matter of better real-time decision-making. He decided to essentially give up on the play.

Daniels also confirmed that he knew a flag had been thrown.

"I did know. I didn't know what it — it could have been offsides, it could have been on us," Daniels said in response to the last question of the session. "You know, I'm not really into that type of stuff, you know?"

The final comment is confusing. Why wouldn't he be "into that type of stuff"? The concept of situational football doesn't end when a play starts. Things can happen during a play that dramatically change the situation.

In this case, the flag created one of two new situations. If the defense was offside, it was a free play. In that situation, Daniels should have taken a shot to the end zone because the penalty always could have been accepted if it didn't work out. If the penalty was on the offense, he still needed to convert.

No one knew what the flag was for, but since there wasn't an obvious jump by the defense (which we see all the time, and which quarterbacks like Aaron Rodgers always use to go for the jugular), the best decision in that situation would have been to try to get the first down, no matter what. The worst decision would have been to just throw the ball out of the end zone, which is the decision Daniels made.

It's another example of an institutional failure to coach Daniels to be ready for all situations and/or a failure of Daniels to want to have all the answers for all possible situations.

Based on Quinn's comments, Daniels got coached about it after the game. Why wasn't he coached about it before the game?

The end result further reveals the tangible flaw in the overall approach to ensuring that the quarterback, the offensive coordinator, and head coach aren't taking a trial-and-error approach to pro football.

Again, it's not on-the-job training. The training happens (or at least it should) during meetings, practices, more meetings, more practices, even more meetings, and even more practices.

All that said, the more reasonable explanation is that Quinn and Daniels didn't know it was fourth down. While not as egregious as what happened at the end of overtime against the Giants, it makes the lingering bad vibes regarding the institutional command of situational football a little bit worse.

item.title: Saints WR Jordyn Tyson will not practice this week
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The wait for Saints wide receiver Jordyn Tyson to make his NFL debut will continue until at least Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
The wait for Saints wide receiver Jordyn Tyson to make his NFL debut will continue until at least Week 9.

General Manager Mickey Loomis told reporters at a Wednesday press conference that the first-round pick will not practice with the team in Paris ahead of this Sunday's game against the Steelers. Tyson has been out since suffering a hamstring injury in mid-August, although head coach Kellen Moore said that it was unrelated to previous hamstring issues while he was in college.

Loomis said that the rookie is improving and "we feel like we're getting closer," but declined to offer a "specific timetable" for him to get on the field.

The Saints have a bye in Week 8, so their Week 9 home game against the Browns will be the earliest possible date for Tyson to join the lineup. Given the length of his absence and history of hamstring issues, a longer ramp up time might be in the cards once Tyson does return to practice.

item.title: Saints GM Mickey Loomis: I understand where Gayle Benson's concerns are coming from
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: "This is an outcome-based sport, and it's not good enough yet," Loomis said.
item.content:encoded:
Saints owner Gayle Benson said last week that the team’s performance has not been acceptable. Saints General Manager Mickey Loomis says he gets it.

"I understood where she's coming from, and I think every once in a while we all need to be a little uncomfortable. That's OK," Loomis said today in Paris, where the Saints will play on Sunday.

Asked about building a winning team, Loomis acknowledged it hasn't happened.

"We haven't done that yet, have we? This is an outcome-based sport, and it's not good enough yet."

Still, Loomis says the Saints' process is good, even if the results haven't been.

"I like the direction we're going," Loomis said. "We're a young, developing team and we have to recognize that. I recognize that. We've got a young coach 22 games into his career. That's where we're at."

Saints quarterback Tyler Shough is showing promise, in Loomis's opinion.

"It all starts with the quarterback and I think we're all excited about him," Loomis said. "There's still a lot of development. He's 13 or 14 games. He hasn't even started a full season yet."

Despite a 2-4 start, Loomis still believes this Saints team can win.

"We didn't get the outcomes that we were expecting or wanted, but they were there ready for us to take them. One of the things about a young team is they have to learn how to win, and we're in that process."

item.title: League reportedly concludes Jalen Hurts's blood clot "was handled appropriately" before Week 5 game
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL, Eagles were and are in lockstep on situation that has many unanswered questions.
item.content:encoded:
To no surprise, the NFL won't be taking any action against the Eagles for its handling of the Jalen Hurts blood clot prior to Hurts playing in Week 5.

While the league has yet to issue a statement to that effect (or to make anyone available for questioning by reporters on the issue), an unnamed source told Jonathan Jones of The Athletic that the NFL has concluded the situation "was handled appropriately" by the team.

It's not a surprise because the Eagles have said, and the league has confirmed, that the team "remained in communication" with the NFL throughout the process. That's the best way to avoid league scrutiny; the Eagles involved the league in the various decisions that were made.

Jones also reports that Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL’s chief medical officer, worked with the Premier League's chief medical officer to have Hurts evaluated at the Cleveland Clinic in London on the evening of Saturday, October 10. The unnamed source told Jones that the team, the staff, the doctors, and Hurts determined he could play the next day against the Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Jones also reiterates the claim, which surfaced after multiple reports claimed Hurts was advised not to sleep, that Hurts "returned to the team hotel around 2:45 a.m. local time Sunday and slept until about 10 a.m.," and that he "took a nap" at the stadium before the game.

The unnamed source also repeats (as the NFL told PFT last week) that the team did not violate the injury reporting rules by, for example, failing to downgrade Hurts to "questionable" the moment his availability was, you know, in question or by failing to disclose that his "calf" injury was in reality a blood clot.

Again, the league's position isn't a surprise. The NFL and the Eagles were and are in lockstep on this issue, which based on the evidence that has been disclosed to date calls into question a lingering cultural reality that healthcare for players seems to be more about checking the boxes required to allow a player to "be available" to play and less about treating the player like any patient who would show up with a problem that requires diagnosis, treatment, and recommended steps to ensure a full and successful return to health, with all other considerations taking a back seat.

Much more should be demanded of the league and its teams on issues like this. So far, however, the NFL Players Association has been conspicuously silent. Many details remain unavailable. Reports from established "insiders" have painted a picture that has been confusing at times, downright bizarre at others.

From the question of whether the league and its teams are truly providing meaningful healthcare to player-patients to the question of whether the league and its teams are creating even more inside information that could be misused for betting purposes (while the millions who are constantly bombarded with gambling ads are kept in the dark regarding the truth as to a player's health), the Hurts case raises very real questions that, with the passing of time, the playing of more regular-season games, and the inevitable emergence of the next story that attracts the media's attention, will fade away and never be adequately answered.

item.title: NFLPA calls for "full investigation" into Jalen Hurts situation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Union issues statement regarding the NFL's handling of the case.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL Players Association has chimed in on the story that the NFL and the Eagles would very much like to see go away.

The NFLPA issued a statement on Tuesday night calling for an investigation into the handling of the Jalen Hurts situation, which resulted in the player traveling to London with a blood clot in his leg, playing with a blood clot in his leg, and traveling back to Philadelphia with a blood clot in his leg.

“The NFLPA is not aware of any NFL investigation into the medical care provided to Jalen Hurts," the union said. "In fact, the league previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care he received. Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward.”

Given that NFL investigations regarding the proper application of the concussion protocol typically take a couple of weeks to resolve, it's odd (to say the least) that the NFL would so quickly conclude that the Hurts situation "was handled appropriately" by the team.

Everything about this situation smacks of a desire to close the book and move on, and to question or criticize anyone who would raise fair and proper questions.

Fortunately, the NFLPA is now among those asking the same questions.

item.title: A.J. Brown sends prayers, support to Jalen Hurts
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Patriots wide receiver A.J.
item.content:encoded:
Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown didn't leave Philadelphia on the best of terms with Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts. But Brown still wishes the best for Hurts, who is out for the season with multiple blood clots in his lungs.

"It’s a tough situation, man," Brown said Tuesday, via Glenn Erby of USA Today. "I've got a lot of love and respect for him, praying for him. I didn't know how serious it was. I think all of us kind of found that out, but he's a tough guy. He's a tough guy, and he can handle anything. . . . He can handle it, and I pray God continue to keep his hand on him. It's a lot of love and respect from this way."

Hurts and Brown played together for four seasons before the Eagles honored the wide receiver's trade request on June 1.

Brown caught 339 passes for 5,034 yards and 32 touchdowns in his four seasons in Philadelphia, making two Pro Bowls and helping the Eagles win a Super Bowl.

Once close, they did not speak after the trade until a joint practice in August.

item.title: Allen Sills dismisses concern about team physician bias as "nonsense" (it's not)
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: When it comes to whether the Eagles properly handled the health care provided to Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts for his blood clots, the NFL is hardly a neutral, disinterested party.
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to whether the Eagles properly handled the health care provided to Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts for his blood clots, the NFL is hardly a neutral, disinterested party. It was the NFL, through chief medical officer Allen Sills, that arranged for the evaluation of Hurts in London, which is part of what the league does to support all NFL teams that are imposed upon to play internationally.

On Tuesday, Sills spoke to reporters at the quarterly ownership meeting in New York. And he arguably protested too much when it comes to lingering concerns about the NFL's culture regarding medical care for players.

"Any idea or any suggestion that a team physician is ever being influenced by a coach, a General Manager, a team owner — it just doesn't happen," Sills insisted. "There is no doctor who is taking orders from a football person, a non-medical person. Period."

Setting aside whether he's directly aware of how all 32 teams operate (he surely isn't), in this context an express order isn't needed. Team-hired doctors understand the assignment; the teams want players to be available to play. In nearly every case, the player wants to be available, too. Any doctor who develops a reputation in the building for being unnecessarily cautious when it comes to clearing a player to play will inevitably be replaced by a doctor who will.

And those assignments are very lucrative, both in what they pay to the doctor and in how they provide the doctor with built-in marketing for the rest of the doctor's practice.

"The notion that there are external factors or that any of our physicians would put a player in harm's way, that's nonsense," Sills said.

The dismissal of that possibility does not mesh with the facts. The mere existence of the Unaffiliated Neurotrauma Consultant program for diagnosing concussions and clearing players to return from concussions directly refutes Sills's contention. If team doctors could be relied upon in every instance to set aside the unspoken (because it doesn't need to be said) urgency to find that a potentially concussed player is good to go or to clear a concussed player to return, there would be NO NEED for doctors with no team affiliation.

As to most other health issues, the situation isn't as critical. Orthopedic injuries don't put a player at risk, and a shot or two of Toradol never hurt anyone, right? (Well, maybe not.)

In those rare instances where the shared desire for the team and the player to "be available" intersects with the player's best interests as a patient, there's inherent pressure on the team-hired doctor to get along by going along.

It's unfortunate that Sills refused to recognize this basic fact. Hopefully, he said it for P.R. purposes and not because he truly believes it.

Finally, Sills invoked "patient privacy concerns" to justify not taking questions about the treatment Hurts received. That's a copout. Hurts has already authorized the issuance of multiple statements that shared with the world various details about his private medical issues.

It's easy to use "patient privacy concerns" as a shield when, in reality, the player quite possibly would authorize doctors to answer any and all questions about a situation that has already become extremely public. At this point, why would Hurts object to his doctors explaining what they did and why they did it?

Through it all, the NFL and the Eagles simply want to move on. All's well that ends, as the late NFL Commissioner Paul Tagliabue liked to say. Hopefully, this one won't end until all necessary questions are asked and answered — and until the NFL recognizes that, for certain health conditions, a UNC-style approach is needed.

item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: C.J.
item.content:encoded:
C.J. Gardner-Johnson isn't the only Bills safety facing a one-game suspension for spitting at a Raiders player during last Sunday's win.

The NFL announced on Wednesday that Sam Franklin has also drawn a suspension for that infraction. Per a release from the league, Franklin spit at an opposing player after the Raiders made an extra point with 1:32 left in the game.

Franklin can appeal the ban and Sal Capaccio of WGR reports that he intends to do so. Capaccio adds that Franklin "vehemently denies" that he spat at a member of the Raiders.

With the Bills on a bye this week, Franklin will miss Buffalo's Week 8 game against the Ravens if the suspension is upheld.

Franklin has played in all six games for the Bills this season and seen all of his action on special teams. He has six tackles in that role.

item.title: Dan Campbell: Packers offense will make plays, we have to make more
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Packers offense had some rocky moments in the opening weeks of the season, but the last two weeks have seen the unit find its footing.
item.content:encoded:
The Packers offense had some rocky moments in the opening weeks of the season, but the last two weeks have seen the unit find its footing.

They've put up 54 points and 746 yards while turning the ball over once in wins over the Bears and Cowboys that have them sitting at 4-2 ahead of Sunday's game in Detroit. The Lions defense had a good showing in its Week 5 game against the Cardinals and they'll be hoping that carries over through last week's bye, but head coach Dan Campbell isn't expecting the group to pitch a shutout.

Campbell called Packers quarterback Jordan Love the team's "secret sauce" during his Tuesday press conference and highlighted the touch he's thrown on deep balls to Christian Watson and Matthew Golden as a particular concern. The two wideouts have 59 catches for 1,039 yards and nine touchdowns on the season, which is why Campbell said the team needs to be prepared to win in a shootout if necessary.

“They’re going to make some plays, but it’s about us making more of ‘em,” Campbell said. “If we get an opportunity for something, we have got to make the most of it, something that swings in our favor. We have to capitalize on those.”

The Packers beat the Lions twice last season and extending that winning streak would push the Lions further into fourth place in a very competitive decision, so Campbell will have to make sure his team is sharp on both sides of the ball this weekend.

item.title: Kevin Byard sharing "as much as I can" with Patriots ahead of return to Chicago
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Patriots safety Kevin Byard isn't from Chicago, but Thursday night's game will still be a homecoming of sorts for the veteran.
item.content:encoded:
Patriots safety Kevin Byard isn't from Chicago, but Thursday night's game will still be a homecoming of sorts for the veteran.

Byard played for the Bears for the last two seasons and was named a first-team All-Pro after helping them win the NFC North last season. Byard moved on as a free agent this offseason, but said he has no bad feelings about his departure and is excited to be back in "an electric environment" at Soldier Field.

The lack of bad feelings doesn't mean he'll do anything he can to give the Patriots a leg up in their bid for a fourth straight win.

“I’m giving the coaches and the players as much as I can, you know what I mean?” Byard said, via Kyle Hightower of the Associated Press. “Obviously, I am not there anymore, and I don’t have all my notes and stuff like that. But as far as personnel, anything I can kind of remember.”

Byard led the league with seven interceptions last season, but he has yet to pick a ball off this year. Getting one off of former teammate Caleb Williams might prove to be a bigger help to New England's cause than any intel Byard might offer off the field.

item.title: Report: Steve Tisch was present for NFL quarterly ownership meetings
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL is having a less-than-ideal week when it comes to optics.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL is having a less-than-ideal week when it comes to optics.

Beyond the ongoing mess arising from the handling and the messaging relating to the health situation involving Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, former Giants co-owner Steve Tisch continues to pop up at team and league events.

The January release of the Epstein files implicated Tisch, through emails he exchanged with Jeffrey Epstein, and created an obvious problem that needed to be investigated. The league vowed to "get the facts first" before deciding whether to discipline Tisch. Then, after Tisch and his siblings transferred their equity into their children's trusts, Commissioner Roger Goodell pointed out when pressed on the inaction that Tisch is no longer an owner.

But Tisch remains the Giants’ chairman of the board. And he was front and center in the draft room in April. The photo attached to this article was taken at the Week 2 Monday night game in L.A.

Most recently, Tisch was present for Tuesday's quarterly ownership meetings in New York, via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports.

The obvious question is why? And the best explanation for the entire situation seems to be that, when the league and the Giants faced a delicate situation regarding what to do about Tisch, someone decided that the right answer was for Tisch to put his equity into trust for his children and otherwise behave as if nothing happened.

And so Tisch is technically out, but he's still very much in. And the paperwork regarding the equity transfer to the people who would have inevitably inherited it anyway gave the NFL the perfect cover not only to take no action but to otherwise turn the page and move on.

That's always the play. Find a way to turn the page and move on. Given the NFL's 365-day news machine (which has allowed this specific outlet to survive for nearly 25 years), there's always a next page.

item.title: Reports: Titans released DT Jordan Elliott after he went to car to get gun
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Multiple reports detail a situation that could have turned into a tragedy.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the Titans abruptly released defensive tackle Jordan Elliott without elaboration as to the "incident" that sparked the move. Multiple reports indicate it was a serious situation that could have gotten a lot worse.

Austin Stanley and Easton Freeze of AtoZSports.com and Aaron Wilson of KPRC in Houston report that Elliott went to his car to get his gun following an altercation on October 15.

Via AtoZSports.com, the Nashville Metro Nashville Police Department said on Tuesday afternoon that no reports had been filed regarding the incident.

Wilson's report adds more details. Per Wilson, Elliott and tackle JC Latham argued after a play. Elliott was then told to leave the practice field. Elliott reportedly went to the players' parking garage to get his gun from his car. Titans defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers de-escalated the situation.

It's unclear whether he actually got the gun and brought it back to the practice field. Presumably he did; if Franklin-Myers had simply stopped Elliott from going to his car, that likely wouldn't have been enough to prompt the Titans to cut Elliott.

Via Wilson, the whole thing was captured by surveillance cameras.

Elliott, 28, had signed a two-year, $8 million contract in the offseason. A third-round pick of the Browns in 2020, he spent four years in Cleveland and two in San Francisco. He played last year for Titans coach Robert Saleh, during Saleh's second, one-year stint as the San Francisco defensive coordinator.

After appearing in the first five games of the 2026 season, Elliott was inactive for Sunday's win over the Colts.

The Titans eventually decided to cut Elliott five days later, and the entire situation had been kept under wraps until the Titans released Elliott without explanation.

It's unclear whether the league was informed of the incident. It would have been prudent, if not mandatory, for the Titans to promptly contact the league office, both to inform them and to seek advice on how to proceed.

item.title: 49ers are the heaviest division favorites in the NFL
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: San Francisco's odds to win the NFC West are at -650
item.content:encoded:
Prior to this season, the NFC West was expected to be the most competitive three-team race in football, with the Rams as the favorites, the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks close behind, and the 49ers a good team but a clear third. Six weeks into the season, things look different.

The 49ers are now 6-0 and the overwhelming favorites to win the NFC West. In fact, with the betting odds at -650, the 49ers are the heaviest favorites to win their division of any team in the league.

The Seahawks are a distant second at +630, the Rams are third at +1200, and the Cardinals are the NFL's longest long shots to win their division at +15,000.

The 49ers have a three-game lead over the 3-3 Seahawks and a four-game lead over the 2-4 Rams and Cardinals, and the 49ers have already beaten all three division rivals head-to-head. It would take something totally unforeseen for the NFC West to end any other way than with the 49ers on top.

The NFL's next-biggest division favorites are the Jaguars at -290 to win the AFC South. The Chiefs are -250 favorites to win the AFC West, the Bills are -200 favorites to win the AFC East, the Panthers are -120 favorites to win the NFC South, the Ravens are -110 favorites to win the AFC North, the Vikings are +105 favorites to win the NFC North and the Cowboys are +130 favorites to win the NFC East.

item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: For each of the past two Super Bowls, the NFL announced the halftime performer in September.
item.content:encoded:
For each of the past two Super Bowls, the NFL announced the halftime performer in September. As October enters the homestretch, there has been no announcement as to Super Bowl LXI in L.A.

On Tuesday, Dave Brooks of Puck reported that Jay-Z, who produces the annual spectacle, has selected himself to do the honors for the next Super Bowl.

Per the report, Justin Bieber and Miley Cyrus also were considered.

The NFL first hired Jay-Z in 2019 to produce the Super Bowl halftime show, with a renewal in 2024. The arrangement reportedly pays $5 million per year.

Brooks notes that Jay-Z could make the announcement this weekend, when he plays a pair of shows at SoFi Stadium, the site of the next Super Bowl. There presumably would be some sort of big splash in conjunction with ESPN/ABC which is televising the Super Bowl.

item.title: NFL looking to play 10 international games in 2027, possibly with one in Asia
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The NFL will play a record nine international games this season.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL will play a record nine international games this season. The league has approval to play up to 10 next season, and NFL executive Peter O'Reilly said that number is being discussed.

“We like continuity, but we are looking at new regions, and Asia would be one of them,” O'Reilly said.

In 2026, the NFL will play in Australia, Brazil, the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Germany and Mexico.

O'Reilly has previously mentioned taking the game to Japan and Italy.

The Saints and Steelers will play the first NFL game in France on Sunday.

item.title: Eagles-Commanders stays in prime time for Week 8
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL reportedly "strongly considered" replacing it with Browns-Steelers.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL considered moving the Week 8 Eagles-Commanders game out of prime time. In the end, the NFL decided to stay put.

Via multiple reports, the rematch of the Week 1 game between NFC East rivals will be televised nationally by NBC and Peacock on Sunday night, November 1.

Rob Tornoe of the Philadelphia Inquirer, who first reported that the NFL was thinking about moving Eagles-Commanders out of the Sunday night spot, reports that the league strongly considered replacing it with Browns at Steelers.

In past years, there has been a rule requiring one of the two home-and-home games between division rivals to be televised on Sunday afternoon. The fact that the league considered moving Browns-Steelers to Sunday after their Week 4 game in Cleveland was played on Thursday night shows that, if the rule still exists, it's more of a guideline.

Either way, it'll be the 2-4 Eagles (who don't have their starting quarterback) and the 1-4-1 Commanders instead of the 4-2 Browns and the 4-2 Steelers in a game that would have featured Mike Tomlin's return to Pittsburgh and Cleveland's reward for claiming first place in the AFC North after six weeks of the 2026 season.

item.title: Rams put Davante Adams, Poona Ford on IR
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Wide receiver Davante Adams is expected to miss the next 6-10 weeks after rupturing his hamstring in last Sunday's loss to the Cardinals and the Rams moved him off of the active roster on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Wide receiver Davante Adams is expected to miss the next 6-10 weeks after rupturing his hamstring in last Sunday's loss to the Cardinals and the Rams moved him off of the active roster on Tuesday.

The Rams announced that Adams and defensive tackle Poona Ford have been placed on injured reserve. Ford is going to miss the rest of the season with a triceps injury.

The only corresponding move was the previously reported signing of kicker Brandon McManus. He replaces Blake Grupe, who was placed on injured reserve Monday due to a torn ACL.

Adams had 30 catches for 480 yards and four touchdowns, so his loss leaves a sizable hole across from Puka Nacua at the top of the team's receiving corps. Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, and Jordan Whittington have 13 combined catches for the Rams this season.

Ford had 15 tackles and a tackle for loss while appearing in all six games this season. Kobie Turner is also expected to miss extended time with a groin injury, but he has not been placed on injured reserve at this point.

item.title: Eagles sign RB Elijah Mitchell to active roster, waive Jaydon Blue and Carson Steele
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Eagles made changes to the running back room on their 53-man roster on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles made changes to the running back room on their 53-man roster on Tuesday.

They announced that they have signed Elijah Mitchell off of their practice squad. They also waived Jaydon Blue and Carson Steele. Steele was waived with an injury designation after hurting his shoulder in Week 6.

Mitchell signed with the Eagles this offseason and returned to the practice squad after being cut in August. He played in one game for the Chiefs last year and ran 327 times for 1,523 yards and nine touchdowns over three seasons with the 49ers.

Blue signed to the active roster ahead of last Sunday's loss to the Panthers, but did not play. Steele had one catch for four yards against Carolina and played in two games overall.

The other backs on the roster are Saquon Barkley and Dameon Pierce. Barkley has missed the last two games with a hamstring injury.

item.title: Patriots CB Carlton Davis upgraded to limited practice participation on Tuesday
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Patriots got cornerback Carlton Davis back at practice on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Patriots got cornerback Carlton Davis back at practice on Tuesday.

Davis was listed as a non-participant on Monday's estimated practice report due to the neck injury that has kept him out of three games this season. Davis has 16 tackles in his three appearances.

Guards Ben Brown (knee) and Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) remained out of practice. Head coach Mike Vrabel said both players are likely to miss Thursday's game against the Bears. Defensive tackle Joshua Farmer (personal) was also listed as a non-participant for the second straight day.

Wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle), cornerback Channing Canada (hamstring), right tackle Morgan Moses (foot), and cornerback Karon Prunty (hamstring) remained in the limited category. Kicker Andy Borregales (personal), offensive tackle Marcus Bryant (ankle), safety Kevin Byard III (chest), offensive tackle Will Campbell (knee), linebacker Christian Elliss (chest), running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle), linebacker Dre’Mont Jones (shoulder), quarterback Drake Maye (right shoulder) and safety Craig Woodson (shoulder) were all listed as full participants.

item.title: Justin Tucker was among five kickers the Dolphins worked out
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Dolphins worked out five kickers after cutting Riley Patterson, who missed an extra point in Week 5 after missing two field goals earlier in the season.
item.content:encoded:
The Dolphins worked out five kickers after cutting Riley Patterson, who missed an extra point in Week 5 after missing two field goals earlier in the season.

They signed Zane Gonzalez.

Among those trying out, though, was former Ravens kicker Justin Tucker, according to the NFL's personnel notice.

Since serving a 10-game suspension for violating the league’s Personal Conduct Policy over sexual misconduct allegations, Tucker has tried out for the Saints, Colts, Jets, and now Dolphins over the past two seasons.

Multiple women accused Tucker of misconduct during massage-therapy sessions. He denied the allegations, and he was never charged criminally or sued civilly.

He has not signed anywhere since, last playing in the league in 2024.

He is a five-time first-team All-Pro, who has made 89.1 percent of his field-goal tries. Tucker, though, converted a career-low 73.3 percent of his field-goal attempts in his last season. He also missed two extra points.

Michael Badgley, Will Ferrin and Joshua Karty were the other kickers who tried out for the Dolphins on Tuesday.
